summary.text: Using that primes beyond 30030 must lie in one of the \(\varphi(30030)=5760\) residue classes coprime to \(30030=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\), the proof derives \(\pi(5M)\le M\) for \(M\ge10^6\), which inductively bounds every term by \(B=10^6+\sum_i v_i\). Consequently only finitely many five-term windows can occur; two must coincide, and determinism of the recurrence propagates that equality forever, giving an eventual positive period.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes less than or equal to \(x\). Given five initial values
\[
v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\in\mathbb N,
\]
define the sequence \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
a_i=v_i\quad(0\le i<5)
\]
and
\[
a_{r+5}=\pi(a_r+a_{r+1}+a_{r+2}+a_{r+3}+a_{r+4})
\quad(r\ge0).
\]
We prove that this sequence is ultimately periodic. In fact, the proof does not use positivity of the initial values, so it proves the stronger assertion for arbitrary nonnegative initial values.

The proof has two parts. First we establish a uniform bound on all terms. Then the ordered windows of five consecutive terms take values in a finite set, so two such windows agree; because the recurrence is deterministic and depends on exactly five preceding terms, that equality propagates forever.

We begin with the prime-counting estimate needed for the uniform bound.

**Prime-counting estimate.** For every integer \(M\ge 1{,}000{,}000\),
\[
\pi(5M)\le M. \tag{1}
\]

For completeness, introduce
\[
\pi_{<}(x)=\#\{p:p\text{ is prime and }p<x\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\pi(x)=\pi_{<}(x+1). \tag{2}
\]
We use a simple residue-class sieve. If \(A>0\), \(K>A\), and \(L\ge0\), then
\[
\pi_{<}(K+L)
 \le \pi_{<}(K)+\varphi(A)\left(\left\lfloor\frac{L}{A}\right\rfloor+1\right), \tag{3}
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function.

Indeed, split the primes below \(K+L\) into those below \(K\) and those in the interval \([K,K+L)\). Every prime \(p\) in the latter interval satisfies \(p\ge K>A\). Such a prime is coprime to \(A\): if a prime \(p>A\) had a common divisor greater than \(1\) with \(A\), then, since the only positive divisors of \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), one would have \(p\mid A\), which is impossible when \(A<p\). Thus the number of primes in \([K,K+L)\) is no greater than the number of integers there which are coprime to \(A\).

Partition that interval into consecutive blocks of length \(A\), followed by at most one partial block. In any block of \(A\) consecutive integers, each residue modulo \(A\) occurs exactly once, and precisely \(\varphi(A)\) of those residues are coprime to \(A\). A partial block contains no more than \(\varphi(A)\) integers coprime to \(A\), because its residues are distinct and there are only \(\varphi(A)\) coprime residue classes. There are \(\lfloor L/A\rfloor\) full blocks and at most one partial block. This proves (3).

Apply (3) with
\[
A=30030=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13,
\qquad K=30031,
\]
and
\[
L=5M+1-30031.
\]
For \(M\ge1{,}000{,}000\), this subtraction is nonnegative and
\[
K+L=5M+1.
\]
Since the six displayed prime factors of \(30030\) are distinct, multiplicativity of the totient gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi(30030)
 &=\varphi(2)\varphi(3)\varphi(5)\varphi(7)\varphi(11)\varphi(13)\\
 &=(2-1)(3-1)(5-1)(7-1)(11-1)(13-1)\\
 &=1\cdot2\cdot4\cdot6\cdot10\cdot12
 =5760. \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
Also, trivially \(\pi_{<}(30031)\le30031\), since there are only \(30031\) nonnegative integers below \(30031\). Therefore (2), (3), and (4) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi(5M)
 &=\pi_{<}(5M+1)\\
 &\le 30031+5760\left(
 \left\lfloor\frac{5M+1-30031}{30030}\right\rfloor+1
 \right). \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
Now
\[
5M+1-30031\le5M,
\]
so, using \(30030=5\cdot6006\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{5M+1-30031}{30030}\right\rfloor
\le \left\lfloor\frac{5M}{30030}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{M}{6006}\right\rfloor. \tag{6}
\]
Set
\[
q=\left\lfloor\frac{M}{6006}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because
\[
6006\cdot166=996996\le1{,}000{,}000\le M,
\]
we have \(q\ge166\). By the defining property of the floor, \(6006q\le M\). Moreover,
\[
30031+5760(q+1)=35791+5760q.
\]
Since \(q\ge166\),
\[
(6006-5760)q=246q\ge246\cdot166=40836\ge35791.
\]
Consequently,
\[
35791+5760q\le6006q\le M. \tag{7}
\]
Combining (5), (6), and (7) proves (1).

We now bound the recurrence. Define
\[
B=1{,}000{,}000+v_0+v_1+v_2+v_3+v_4. \tag{8}
\]
Then \(B\ge1{,}000{,}000\). We claim that
\[
a_n\le B\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0. \tag{9}
\]
We prove this by strong induction on \(n\).

For \(n=0,1,2,3,4\), one has \(a_n=v_n\), and each \(v_n\) is at most the sum on the right side of (8), hence at most \(B\).

Now let \(n=r+5\), and suppose that all earlier terms are at most \(B\). In particular,
\[
a_r,a_{r+1},a_{r+2},a_{r+3},a_{r+4}\le B,
\]
so
\[
a_r+a_{r+1}+a_{r+2}+a_{r+3}+a_{r+4}\le5B. \tag{10}
\]
The prime-counting function is nondecreasing: if \(x\le y\), every prime at most \(x\) is also at most \(y\). Hence, by the recurrence, (10), and estimate (1) applied with \(M=B\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{r+5}
 &=\pi(a_r+a_{r+1}+a_{r+2}+a_{r+3}+a_{r+4})\\
 &\le\pi(5B)\\
 &\le B.
\end{aligned}
\]
This completes the strong induction and proves (9).

Next we record why equality of two five-term windows forces equality forever. Suppose that \(N,P\ge0\) and
\[
a_{N+P+i}=a_{N+i}\qquad(0\le i<5). \tag{11}
\]
We claim that
\[
a_{N+P+t}=a_{N+t}\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0. \tag{12}
\]
Again use strong induction on \(t\). For \(t<5\), this is exactly (11). If \(t\ge5\), write \(t=k+5\). Each of the offsets
\[
k,k+1,k+2,k+3,k+4
\]
is strictly smaller than \(t\), so the induction hypothesis gives
\[
a_{N+P+k+j}=a_{N+k+j}\qquad(0\le j<5).
\]
Therefore the sums of the five preceding terms at positions \(N+P+k+5\) and \(N+k+5\) are equal. Applying \(\pi\) to those equal sums and using the defining recurrence yields
\[
a_{N+P+k+5}=a_{N+k+5}.
\]
Thus (12) follows.

It remains to find two equal windows. For each \(n\ge0\), form the ordered five-tuple
\[
W_n=(a_n,a_{n+1},a_{n+2},a_{n+3},a_{n+4}).
\]
By (9), every coordinate of every \(W_n\) lies in the finite set
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,B\}.
\]
Hence the windows \(W_n\) lie in the finite set \(\{0,1,\ldots,B\}^5\), which has \((B+1)^5\) elements. Since there are infinitely many indices \(n\), the pigeonhole principle supplies two distinct indices \(m,n\) for which
\[
W_m=W_n.
\]
Interchanging the two indices if necessary, assume \(m<n\), and set
\[
N=m,\qquad P=n-m.
\]
Then \(P>0\), and \(N+P=n\). Equality of the windows says precisely that
\[
a_{N+P+i}=a_{N+i}\qquad(0\le i<5).
\]
By the propagation result (12),
\[
a_{N+P+t}=a_{N+t}\qquad(t\ge0). \tag{13}
\]
Finally, if \(q\ge N\), put \(t=q-N\). Then \(q=N+t\), and (13) gives
\[
a_{q+P}=a_q.
\]
Thus there exist \(N\ge0\) and \(P>0\) such that
\[
a_{q+P}=a_q\qquad\text{for every }q\ge N.
\]
This is exactly ultimate periodicity, completing the proof.
